name: Mapun
confidence_why: 5 independent first-hand descriptions agree (3 state the same rule, 1 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: When a suffix is added to a word with a long vowel so that the long vowel lies in the stressed syllable (the next-to-last syllable of the word), the line over the vowel need not be written, since the stress gives the vowel its equivalent of length in pronunciation. hāp 'good' ka- + hāp + -an = kahapan 'goodness' [p. 8, sec. 5.5; scanned renders hāp as 'hdp'] ... [fn. 2, p. 8:] Some have been heard to pronounce these words, babahan and hatuhun, so it appears that between like-vowels, /h/ tends to weaken in force, occasioning a long-sounding vowel, which in turn makes the word sound like it has word-final stress, instead of penultimate stress.
new_statements.citation: Collins, Millard A., Virginia R. Collins & Sulfilix A. Hashim (comps.). 2001. Mapun-English dictionary. Manila: Summer Institute of Linguistics - Philippines. viii+683 pp.
new_statements.locator: Front matter sec. 5 'A Guide to Spelling Mapun Words': p. 8, sec. 5.5 'Lengthening of vowels' and p. 8 fn. 2 (PDF page 5 of); also p. 7, sec. 5.4.1. The open_url scan (rosettaproject_sjm_morsyn-1, sec. 7 'Grammar Notes', pp. 17-47) contains no stress statement.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (8 pp., title 'Mapun Orthography'; title page reads 'MAPUN-ENGLISH DICTIONARY, compiled by Millard A. Collins, Virginia R. Collins, Mapun Language Consultant Sulfilix A. Hashim, SIL-Philippines 2001'). extracted text page 5 carries the running head '8.. Spelling Mapun Words' and contains, word for word, 'When a suffix is added to a word with a long vowel so that the long vowel lies in the stressed syllable (the next-to-last syllable of the word), the line over the vowel need not be written, since the stress gives the vowel its equivalent of length in pronunciation.' followed by the example line and, at the foot of the page, fn. 2: 'Some have been heard to pronounce these words, babah…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (penultimate stress = penultimate). Adds that the penult is computed over the suffixed word (suffixes are inside the stress window), that stress lengthens the penult vowel, and the /h/-weakening note on apparent final stress. The statement sits in the orthography guide, not a dedicated phonology section; the Grammar Notes scan at the open_url is silent on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, and it is recomputed on the suffixed word (hāp 'good' > kahápan 'goodness'): the stress domain includes suffixes. Long vowels are written with a macron except where they land in the stressed penult, since stress itself lengthens that vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 2, p. 8: when /h/ between like vowels weakens (babahan, hatuhun) the resulting long vowel makes the word 'sound like it has word-final stress, instead of penultimate stress' - a phonetic effect the authors present as apparent, not as a different stress rule. Sec. 5.4.1, p. 7: base-final vowels drop before -an/-un (awon > awnan, dilawut > padilawtan) because keeping them 'would oblige' readers 'to stress a syllable.. that has been completely dropped out in speech', i.e. stress is assigned to the surface penult of the affixed form.
new_statements.identity_note: Collins et al. 2001 describes Mapun (Jama Mapun, Cagayan de Sulu; ISO sjm) itself. The Pallesen 1985 SIL record is catalogued under Central Sama [sml]; the widely quoted penultimate-stress line attributed to Pallesen 1985:124 (via Wikipedia) concerns the Sinama/Sama-Bajaw languages as a group, not Mapun specifically.

new_statements.quote: [sec. 3.5 STRESS, p. 94:] Primary stress in PSB occurs regularly on the vowel of the penultimate syllable of the word, reconstructed on the basis of its reflex on the penult in all SB languages except in predictable environments in NB. This observation applies to words, not merely to stems, so that suffixation results in the shif[t] of stress to the right. [...] In NB stress occurs on the penult except when the vowel of the penult is the mid central vowel /ə/, in which case it occurs on the ultima. [Appendix I, p. 277:] Note that stress in all Sama-Bajaw languages falls on the penult, with rare exceptions which are indicated. [I.1.8 Jama Mapun (JM), p. 282: no exception indicated.] (scanned text layer is letter-spaced; spacing normalized, schwa restored from scanned '/a/')
new_statements.citation: Pallesen, A. Kemp. 1985. Culture contact and language convergence. (Linguistic Society of the Philippines Special Monograph 24.) Manila: LSP. xxix+365 pp.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog codes Mapun fixed-dominant penult (penultimate stress) and the statement held by the project (Collins, Collins & Hashim 2001, penultimate, suffixes shift stress) says the same; Pallesen 1985 states penultimate word stress for all Sama-Bajaw languages including JM, with rightward shift under suffixation, and flags no Mapun exception. The statement is family-wide (PSB and 'all SB languages') rather than a Mapun-specific description, as the compilers anticipated, but JM is explicitly among the languages covered and the JM-specific p. 79 remark presupposes it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Proto-Sama-Bajaw and in all Sama-Bajaw daughter languages (Jama Mapun = JM included; the only stated exception class is Sabah Land Bajaw NB), primary stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word; the domain is the whole word, so suffixes shift stress rightward onto the new penult. Appendix I repeats that stress in all SB languages is penultimate with rare exceptions marked in the data, and the Jama Mapun entry marks none. The p. 79 remark that JM reduces a to a schwa-like allophone 'in the syllable before primary stress' presupposes the same fixed (penultimate) primary stress in JM.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none stated (the work speaks only of primary stress; p. 51 and p. 79 mention loss/reduction of vowel contrast in the syllable before primary stress in NB, YK and JM, not a secondary stress)
new_statements.exceptions: Only for NB (Sabah Land Bajaw): stress on the ultima when the penult vowel is schwa, with degemination (sec. 3.5, p. 94; sec. 3.7 list p. 115 'stress shift from penult to ultima, unique to NB'). No exception is indicated for Jama Mapun. Suffixation moves stress to the new penult (example paradigm from CS.2 Sama Dilaut).
new_statements.identity_note: Pallesen treats Mapun as 'Jama Mapun (JM)', self-designation 'Pallun mapun', Cagayan Sulu (Mapun) Island and southern Palawan, from his own 372-word list and text plus Casino's and Forman's material; the stress statement itself is family-level (Proto-Sama-Bajaw and all SB daughter languages) with a Central Sama (CS.2 Sama Dilaut) example, and one JM-specific remark (p. 79) on pretonic vowel reduction presupposes the same penultimate primary stress.

audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: Coding (fixed penultimate, penultimate stress, dominant not strict) is supported by every source opened, but the record's only citation is a Wikipedia family-article sentence about the Sinama (Inner Sulu) languages, third-hand from Pallesen 1985:124, with empty cite/loc/grade fields; Mapun is classified as Borneo Coast Bajaw, so that sentence does not strictly cover it. Mapun-specific confirmation now obtained: SIL's own Mapun Dictionary web edition Grammar page ('stress is on the penultimate syllable') and a page explicitly summarising Collins et al. 2001 ('Mapun words have predictable stress on the penultimate syllable'); Kaufman's handbook chapter confirms right-aligned trochaic stress with suffixes/enclitics inside the window for SB generally. No grammar, phonology paper or acoustic study of Mapun exists (Glottolog 0 descriptive refs; Ingilan & Jubilado say no reference grammar; SIL arc
audit.second_reader_evidence: Quote finding verified: we have no copy; the record's only source is Wikipedia 'Mapun language' -> redirect 'Sama–Bajaw languages', Stress section, verbatim 'all of the Sinama languages primary stress occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word.[3]:124 Stress will remain on the penultimate syllable even with the addition of suffixes including enclitic pronouns' (saved) — a Sinama-scope, third-hand statement; cite/loc/grade empty. the compilers readings of its downloaded files also check out verbatim: SIL Webonary Mapun Dictionary Grammar page 'Typology: VSO; stress is on the penultimate syllable' (Phonology page empty); iloko.tripod

sources.quote: 'No SB language shows the phonemic vowel length distinction in penultimate syllables characteristic of Philippine languages. Rather, most SB languages have been described as having a right-aligned trochaic, stress pattern. Some varieties, such as Pangutaran Sama, have been further described as having iterative secondary stress preceding the primary stress on the penultimate syllable (Pallesen 1979:192). The stress window includes suffixes and genitive pronominal enclitics.' Family-level; Mapun not singled out.
sources.locator: sec. 2, p.3, with ex. (2) from Pallesen 1985:94
